reason: The sources provide multi-site verification for over a dozen specific claims detailing the 2018 spectroscopic discovery of hydrogen sulfide in Uranus's atmosphere.
story: For decades after Voyager 2 swept past Uranus in 1986, astronomers were baffled by the hidden chemistry of the planet's pale cyan clouds. In April 2018, an international research team finally solved the mystery using the 8-meter Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea. Analyzing reflected infrared sunlight, they confirmed that Uranus's upper cloud tops are permeated with hydrogen sulfide—the noxious molecule that gives rotten eggs their signature stench. Unlike Jupiter and Saturn, where ammonia ice dominates the cloud tops, Uranus formed in the colder outer reaches of the early solar system, locking away frozen sulfur. But if you picture an overpowering cosmic stench, human senses would never register it. Uranus's atmosphere is an inhospitable cocktail of hydrogen, helium, and methane plunged to minus 200 degrees Celsius; any unprotected visitor would freeze solid and suffocate long before catching a single whiff.
angle: Uranus's upper clouds are confirmed to be permeated with rotten egg gas, but the minus 200°C atmosphere would suffocate and freeze you long before you could smell it.

claims.claim: In April 2018, astronomers reported conclusive evidence that hydrogen sulfide gas is present in Uranus's upper cloud deck.
The research findings confirming hydrogen sulfide on Uranus were published in the journal Nature Astronomy.
Hydrogen sulfide is the chemical compound responsible for the pungent odor of rotten eggs.
The detection was made using the 8-meter Gemini North telescope located on Mauna Kea in Hawaii.
Patrick Irwin of the University of Oxford served as the lead author of the discovery team.
Leigh Fletcher of the University of Leicester was a co-author on the research study.
Glenn Orton of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory was a co-author on the research study.
The team obtained the crucial data using the Near-Infrared Integral Field Spectrometer (NIFS) on Gemini North.
The spectrometer measured reflected sunlight immediately above Uranus's main visible cloud layer.
The spectroscopic absorption lines for hydrogen sulfide were extremely faint and near the edge of detection.
The discovery resolved a long-standing debate over whether hydrogen sulfide or ammonia dominated Uranus's upper cloud deck.
Decades of previous telescopic observations and NASA's 1986 Voyager 2 flyby had failed to conclusively identify the composition of Uranus's clouds.
Uranus's cloud tops differ from Jupiter and Saturn, where ammonia ice is observed above the clouds and hydrogen sulfide is absent.
Hydrogen sulfide freezes at lower temperatures than ammonia, indicating Uranus formed farther from the Sun than Jupiter and Saturn.
The atmosphere of Uranus is composed primarily of hydrogen, helium, and methane.
The temperature of Uranus's upper atmosphere drops to approximately minus 200 degrees Celsius.
According to study lead Patrick Irwin, exposure and suffocation in Uranus's atmosphere would kill a human long before they could smell the gas.

disputed: The exact altitude and pressure level of Uranus's upper cloud decks remain model-dependent; older radio occultation placed methane cloudtops at 1.2–1.3 bar and lower clouds at 3 bar, whereas newer near-infrared analyses place them between 1–3 bar and up to 6 bar. Scripts should refer broadly to 'the cloud tops' rather than citing a single disputed bar depth.
